This chunk is about:
- Cases: Slaughter-House Cases; Ward v. Maryland; United States v. Harris; United States v. Darby Lumber Co.
- Concepts: Fourteenth Amendment; Privileges or Immunities Clause; Privileges and Immunities Clause; Commerce Clause; early civil rights law; freedom of movement under United States law; state authority; employment regulation

Facts:
- Ward v. Maryland, 79 U.S. 418, was decided in 1871 and was later cited as part of a line of cases on the privileges and immunities issue.
- The Slaughter-House Cases, 83 U.S. 36, were decided in 1873 and became a pivotal case in early civil rights law.
- The Slaughter-House Cases held that the Fourteenth Amendment protects the privileges or immunities of citizenship of the United States rather than the privileges and immunities of state citizenship.
- United States v. Harris, 106 U.S. 629, was decided in 1883 and was cited as part of the Court’s consistent position that authority under the privileges and immunities clause was given to the states.
- United States v. Darby Lumber Co., 312 U.S. 100, was decided in 1941.
- United States v. Darby Lumber Co. upheld the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.
- United States v. Darby Lumber Co. held that the U.S. Congress has power under the Commerce Clause to regulate employment conditions.
- Freedom of movement under United States law describes the Court as consistently holding through cases such as Ward v. Maryland, the Slaughter-House Cases, and United States v. Harris that authority under the privileges and immunities clause was given to the states.
